description: Atman, Brahman, samsara, maya, moksha and how karma shapes rebirth and liberation.
content_html:
The Eternal Self: Atman

At the heart of Hindu belief is the conviction that every living being possesses an atman — an eternal self that has no beginning and no end. The atman is not the body, the mind or the personality. It is the unchanging reality within each person, described in the Bhagavad Gita as that which “weapons cannot cut, fire cannot burn, water cannot wet, and wind cannot dry” (Bhagavad Gita II 23). The atman simply is: unborn, undying and indestructible.

Hindus hold different views about the relationship between atman and Brahman, the ultimate reality. The Advaita Vedanta school, associated with the philosopher Shankara, teaches that atman and Brahman are identical — there is ultimately only one reality, and the self is that reality. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (III 7 15–23) describes Brahman as the “inner controller” dwelling within all things. In contrast, the Vishishtadvaita school (associated with Ramanuja) holds that the individual self is real and distinct from Brahman, although part of Brahman’s being. These are genuinely different understandings with practical consequences: if atman equals Brahman, liberation means realising this identity; if atman is distinct, liberation means loving union with a personal God.

Key Fact

The Bhagavad Gita II 23 describes the atman as eternal and indestructible, using the image of a person changing worn-out clothes for new ones to explain how the soul passes from body to body at death.

Samsara: The Cycle of Rebirth

Samsara is the endless cycle of birth, life, death and rebirth. Hindus believe the atman does not die when the body dies; it is reborn into a new body. The form of that new birth — whether as a human, an animal or in a heavenly or lower realm — is determined by the quality of actions performed in previous lives. Samsara is therefore not simply a neutral cycle: it is driven by karma and shaped by the choices each person makes.

Hindu teaching holds that a person reaps what they have sown across many lifetimes. This idea gives each life a profound moral weight: how a person lives now has consequences that extend far beyond a single existence.

Maya: The Veil of Illusion

Maya is the concept that the material world, while real in one sense, obscures the deeper truth of Brahman. Maya causes people to identify with their bodies, possessions and social roles rather than with their eternal atman. Shankara compared maya to a person who mistakes a rope for a snake in dim light: the mistake feels very real but is corrected once light appears. Attachment to the world produced by maya is what keeps the atman bound in samsara.

Recognising maya for what it is requires detachment — the practice of not clinging to material things, outcomes or relationships as if they were the ultimate source of happiness. Detachment does not mean withdrawing from life; it means acting wholeheartedly while releasing one’s grip on results. The Bhagavad Gita (II 11–13) encourages warriors (and, by extension, all people) to carry out their duty without attachment to victory or loss. This teaching is foundational to the path of karma yoga.

Some rare individuals are described as jivan mukti — liberated while still in a physical body. These are individuals who have overcome maya and realised their true nature. Their actions no longer accumulate karma because they act without any sense of ego-ownership.

Karma: Cosmic Justice in Action

The word karma means ‘action’, but in Hindu theology it refers to the moral law of cause and effect. Every action — physical, verbal or mental — generates karma: positive consequences from good actions, negative consequences from harmful ones. Karma is not punishment from a deity; it is an impersonal cosmic law, like gravity. The Bhagavad Gita (III 3–9) describes how all living beings in the material world are compelled to act, and that it is therefore essential to act rightly.

Hindu thought distinguishes between two types of karma already in motion. Parabdha karma is the portion of past karma that is bearing fruit in the current lifetime — it cannot be avoided, only lived through. Kriyamana karma is the karma being created right now by present choices; this is where moral freedom lies.

Key Fact

Parabdha karma is already ‘in flight’ from past actions and shapes the current life. Kriyamana karma is being created now through present choices. Only kriyamana karma can be influenced in the present moment.

Sakam and Nishkam Karma

The Bhagavad Gita (III 3–9) draws a crucial distinction between two ways of acting. Sakam karma means action performed with a desired result in mind — the person seeks personal gain, reward or recognition. Such action binds the atman more firmly to samsara because it feeds desire. Nishkam karma means desireless action: doing what duty requires without attachment to the outcome. The Gita teaches this as the highest form of action, the key to liberation.

Many students think karma simply means ‘what goes around comes around’ in a single lifetime. Hindu teaching is more complex: karma accumulates across many lifetimes and can only be fully exhausted through either living it out or achieving liberation. Karma is also not about fate: humans retain free will and are always making choices (kriyamana karma) that shape the future. The cycle of samsara driven by karma is something to be transcended, not simply accepted.

Moksha: Liberation from Samsara

Moksha is the final goal of Hindu life: liberation from samsara and the end of the cycle of rebirth. For Advaita Vedanta, moksha means the realisation that atman is Brahman — the dissolving of the illusion of a separate self into the infinite. For Vaishnava traditions, moksha is more like eternal loving relationship with a personal God. Either way, moksha ends the accumulation of karma and the need to be reborn. It is described not as annihilation but as the fullest realisation of what the atman truly is.
exam_tip_html: When a question says ‘Outline’ or ‘Describe’, examiners want accurate content with no evaluation — save your judgements for ‘Explain’ and ‘Discuss’ questions. A very common error on this topic is confusing karma with fate: always make clear that karma involves moral choice and is not simply predetermined. For the 15-mark Discuss, name both Advaita Vedanta (atman = Brahman) and Vaishnava views to show genuine religious diversity. Spell technical terms accurately: ‘atman’, ‘moksha’, ‘samsara’, ‘nishkam karma’ — SPaG is assessed on extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The atman is the eternal self within every being; it is indestructible (Bhagavad Gita II 23) and its relationship with Brahman is understood differently by different Hindu schools — as identical (Advaita Vedanta) or as distinct but part of Brahman (Vishishtadvaita).
  • Samsara is the cycle of rebirth driven by karma; maya (illusion) keeps the atman trapped in this cycle by making the material world appear to be ultimate reality.
  • Karma is the moral law of cause and effect; nishkam (desireless) karma frees the atman while sakam (result-seeking) karma binds it further to samsara; the goal is moksha — liberation.

practice_questions.text: State what the term 'atman' means in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: The eternal self or soul present within every living being. [1 mark]

Students may include: the continuous cycle of birth, death and rebirth; the atman is reborn into a new body after death; the form of rebirth is determined by karma; the cycle continues until the atman achieves moksha/liberation. [2 marks — 1 for a simple statement, 2 for a developed description]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Hindu teaching about karma as a form of cosmic justice.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: karma means 'action' and refers to the moral law of cause and effect; every action generates consequences across lifetimes; good actions produce positive karma, harmful actions produce negative karma; it is not punishment from a deity but an impersonal law; the Bhagavad Gita (III 3-9) teaches that all beings must act and should do so rightly; parabdha karma is already bearing fruit while kriyamana karma is being created by present choices. [3 marks — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a well-outlined account with specific detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain two different Hindu understandings of the relationship between atman and Brahman.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Advaita Vedanta (Shankara): atman and Brahman are identical; there is ultimately one reality; the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (III 7 15-23) describes Brahman as the inner controller; liberation means realising this identity.
• Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja): atman is real and distinct from Brahman but part of Brahman's being; liberation means loving union with a personal God rather than complete merger.
• The distinction matters practically: Advaita aims at loss of separate self; Vaishnava traditions aim at eternal relationship with God.
[6 marks — 3 marks per understanding: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a well-explained account with specific detail or source]

practice_questions.text: 'The concept of maya makes it impossible for Hindus to live meaningfully in the material world.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments that could support the statement: if the material world is maya (illusion), attachments and goals in it may seem pointless; Advaita teaching that only Brahman is ultimately real could lead to withdrawal from social and moral responsibility; some ascetics do renounce worldly life entirely as a response to maya.

Arguments that could challenge the statement: maya does not mean the world is unreal, only that it is not the ultimate reality; detachment (as taught in Bhagavad Gita II 11-13) means acting without clinging to results, not refusing to act; nishkam karma teaches engaged, dutiful action in the world without self-seeking; jivan mukti shows liberation is compatible with remaining in the world; many Hindus live very actively in society guided by dharma, artha and kama alongside moksha.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita II 11-13, III 3-9; Shankara vs Ramanuja debate), explicit weighing of the arguments, and a justified conclusion explaining why the statement is an oversimplification.
Secure: two clear perspectives with some use of Hindu teaching, conclusion present.
Developing: one side more developed than the other; some relevant content; limited use of sources.
Emerging: one-sided or very brief; little specific Hindu content.

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between sakam karma and nishkam karma.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: sakam karma is action performed with a desired result in mind; the person seeks personal gain, reward or recognition; such action binds the atman more firmly to samsara; nishkam karma is desireless action performed without attachment to the outcome; it is taught in the Bhagavad Gita (III 3-9) as the highest form of action; nishkam karma leads towards liberation while sakam karma increases bondage. [3 marks — 1 for naming the distinction, 2 for describing one type, 3 for a full account of both with the implication for rebirth/liberation]

knowledge_checks.q: What does the term 'atman' refer to in Hinduism?
options: The cycle of birth and rebirth
The eternal, indestructible self within every being
The illusion created by the material world
The liberation achieved at the end of samsara

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of karma cannot be avoided because it is already bearing fruit in the current lifetime?
Maya is the concept that the material world obscures the deeper truth of _____, causing people to identify with their bodies rather than their eternal atman.
A person who has achieved liberation while still in a physical body is described in Hinduism as _____.
Match each Hindu term to its correct meaning:
right: The continuous cycle of birth, death and rebirth
Liberation from the cycle of samsara
Desireless action performed without attachment to outcomes

flashcard_questions.a: The eternal, indestructible self within every living being.

flashcard_questions.q: What image does Bhagavad Gita II 23 use to explain how the atman moves between bodies?
flashcard_questions.a: Changing worn-out clothes for new ones.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Advaita Vedanta understand the relationship between atman and Brahman?
flashcard_questions.a: They are identical — there is ultimately only one reality.
The endless cycle of rebirth that the atman undergoes until karma is exhausted through moksha.
The illusion that makes the material world appear to be ultimate reality.
Karma already bearing fruit in the current lifetime, which cannot be avoided.
Karma being created right now by a person's present choices.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between sakam and nishkam karma?
flashcard_questions.a: Sakam is action seeking a result; nishkam is desireless action without attachment to outcomes.

flashcard_questions.q: Which text teaches that all beings must act and should do so without desire for results?
flashcard_questions.a: The Bhagavad Gita, especially chapters II and III.
Liberation from samsara and the end of the cycle of rebirth.
Liberation achieved while still alive in a physical body.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does nishkam karma lead towards moksha while sakam karma does not?
flashcard_questions.a: Desireless action creates no new karmic bondage; result-seeking action deepens attachment to samsara.

glossary_terms.definition: The eternal self or soul present within every living being; the true identity of a person beneath the physical body.
The universal, ultimate reality or supreme consciousness that underlies all existence.
The continuous cycle of birth, death and rebirth that all living beings are caught up in until they achieve liberation.
Illusion or the power that makes the material world appear to be the ultimate reality, obscuring the true nature of Brahman.
Action, and the moral law of cause and effect that links every action to its future consequences across lifetimes.
A person who has achieved liberation from samsara while still alive; literally 'liberated while living'.
Liberation from the cycle of samsara; the ultimate goal of Hindu life, achieved when the atman is freed from karma and rebirth.
